Main set

#1multiple-choicefrom Q1inquiry 5.1
ext3-q1-hockey-trajectory.png
The dashed line shows the path of a hockey ball scooped into the air, moving from A to D. At which of the labelled positions is the ball's acceleration directed vertically downward?
  • ✓ At all four positions A, B, C and D
  • At D only
  • At C and D only
  • At B, C and D only
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Once the ball leaves the stick, the only force on it is gravity, which acts straight down at every point of the flight.
#2true-falsefrom Q2inquiry 5.1
ext3-q2-strobe-balls.png
The strobe diagram shows a black ball dropped from rest and a white ball projected horizontally, released at the same instant. The diagram shows that at each flash the two balls are at the same height and have fallen the same distance.
  • ✓ True
  • False
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Horizontal and vertical motion are independent; the horizontal launch of the white ball does not change how it falls.
#3numeric-entryfrom Q4inquiry 5.2
ext3-q4-banked-curve.png
For the frictionless banked curve shown, calculate the maximum safe speed in m s$^{-1}$. Take $g = 9.8$ m s$^{-2}$.
11.5m s^{-1}
accepted within ±3% (relative)
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Read the radius (63 m) and banking angle (12 degrees) from the diagram, then use $v = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$.
#4multiple-choicefrom Q6inquiry 6.2
ext3-q6-current-loop.png
For the current-carrying loop WXYZ in the magnetic field shown (field lines up the page, current direction marked), what are the directions of the forces on sides WZ and XY?
  • ✓ Force on WZ is into the page; force on XY is out of the page
  • Force on WZ is out of the page; force on XY is into the page
  • Both forces are into the page
  • Both forces are out of the page
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Apply $F = I\vec{L} \times \vec{B}$ to each side; the currents in WZ and XY run in opposite directions, so the forces are opposite, giving a torque.
#5multiple-choicefrom Q7inquiry 6.3
ext3-q7-flux-diagrams.png
The two diagrams contain the same number of magnetic field lines, but the left-hand region is smaller. Which statement is correct?
  • ✓ Both show the same magnetic flux, and the smaller region has the greater flux density
  • Both show the same flux and the same flux density
  • The smaller region shows less flux and a lower flux density
  • The smaller region shows more flux and a lower flux density
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Flux is the total number of field lines; flux density is that number divided by the area they pass through.
#6numeric-entryfrom Q8inquiry 5.2
ext3-q8-spanner.png
Using the spanner length, force and angle shown in the diagram, calculate the magnitude of the torque applied to the nut.
32.9N m
accepted within ±3% (relative)
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): $\tau = rF\sin\theta = 0.500 \times 70.0 \times \sin 70^\circ$.
#7numeric-entryfrom Q9inquiry 6.2
ext3-q9-three-rods.png
Using the currents and separations shown for the three parallel rods, calculate the magnitude of the net force per unit length on rod C. Use $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ N A$^{-2}$.
1e-05N m^{-1}
accepted within ±6% (relative)
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Rod B carries current the same way as C (attraction, 0.20 m away); rod A carries it the opposite way (repulsion, 0.30 m away). Work out $\dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi r}$ for each and combine.
#8multiple-choicefrom Q9binquiry 6.2
ext3-q9-three-rods.png
In which direction does the net force per unit length on rod C act?
  • ✓ Towards rod B (up the page)
  • Towards rod A (down the page)
  • Along the length of rod C
  • There is no net force on rod C
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Rod B attracts C (same current direction) and is closer than rod A, which repels C, so B's pull wins.
#9multiple-choicefrom Q10inquiry 6.3
ext3-q10-rod-on-rails.png
The conducting rod slides to the right along the rails, through a magnetic field directed into the page. Which row is correct?
  • ✓ Force on the rod: to the left. Induced current in the rod: upward. Current around the loop: anticlockwise
  • Force to the left; current downward in the rod; clockwise around the loop
  • Force to the right; current upward in the rod; anticlockwise around the loop
  • Force to the right; current downward in the rod; clockwise around the loop
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): The area of the loop, and so the flux into the page, is increasing; the induced current opposes that increase, and the force opposes the rod's motion.
#10drag-dropfrom Q11inquiry 5.2
ext3-q11-whirling-stopper.png
In the apparatus shown, the rubber stopper is swung in a horizontal circle on a string that runs through the tube to a hanging mass. The swing rate is adjusted until the hanging mass neither rises nor falls, then the radius is measured. Match each quantity to its role in the investigation.
Rate of rotation of the stopper→Independent variable
Radius of the circular path→Dependent variable
Mass of the rubber stopper→Controlled variable
Length of the string→Controlled variable
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): The quantity deliberately changed is independent; the one then measured is dependent; anything held fixed is controlled.
#11multiple-choicefrom Q13inquiry 7.2
ext3-q13-double-slit.png
In the double-slit set-up shown, the distance between the slits and the screen is increased while everything else stays the same. What happens to the spacing between the bright bands?
  • ✓ It increases
  • It decreases
  • It stays the same
  • The bright bands disappear
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Fringe spacing $\Delta y = \dfrac{\lambda L}{d}$ is directly proportional to the slit-to-screen distance $L$.
#12true-falsefrom Q13binquiry 7.2
ext3-q13-double-slit.png
If instead the separation between the two slits were increased (with the screen distance unchanged), the spacing between the bright bands would decrease.
  • ✓ True
  • False
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): $\Delta y = \dfrac{\lambda L}{d}$ is inversely proportional to the slit separation $d$.
#13numeric-entryfrom Q15inquiry 7.2
ext3-q15-polarisers.png
Unpolarised light of intensity 150 W m$^{-2}$ passes through polariser P1 (axis 30 degrees to the vertical) and then P2 (axis horizontal), as shown. Calculate the intensity transmitted through P2.
18.75W m^{-2}
accepted within ±3% (relative)
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): P1 halves the intensity to 75 W m$^{-2}$; the angle between P1 and P2 is 60 degrees, so $I = 75\cos^2 60^\circ$.
#14numeric-entryfrom Q19inquiry 8.3
ext3-q19-mercury-levels.png
Using the mercury energy-level diagram, calculate the frequency of the photon emitted when an electron falls from the n = 5 level to the n = 3 level. Use $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}$ J s and $1$ eV $= 1.602 \times 10^{-19}$ J.
440000000000000.0Hz
accepted within ±4% (relative)
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Read the two level energies from the diagram ($-3.71$ eV and $-5.52$ eV); the photon energy is their difference, 1.81 eV, then $f = E/h$.
#15multiple-choicefrom Q20inquiry 8.2
ext3-q20-atomic-models.png
Model 1 and Model 2 show alpha particles passing through two models of the atom. Which option correctly identifies the models?
  • ✓ Model 1 is Thomson's model (alpha particles barely deflected by the spread-out charge); Model 2 is Rutherford's model (a few alpha particles deflected sharply by a tiny dense nucleus)
  • Model 1 is Rutherford's model; Model 2 is Thomson's model
  • Both diagrams show Rutherford's nuclear model
  • Both diagrams show Thomson's plum-pudding model
💡 Tip (shown only if the student answers incorrectly): Only a small, dense, concentrated positive charge can push an alpha particle through a large angle.
